title: Satellites Watch the Sea
objective: After this level you can explain how satellites measure the ocean.
summary: Radar altimeters time echoes to measure sea height to a few centimeters. Other sensors read temperature and color, and Argo floats measure below.

cards.headline: Sea level isn't level: the Pacific sits about 20 cm above the Atlantic.
cards.body: Pacific water is usually warmer and fresher, so it's less dense and stands a little taller, just as Level 6's layers would predict. But how do you measure a 20 cm hill spread across an ocean? From space.

cards.headline: Timing echoes from orbit
cards.body: Sonar times a sound pulse's echo underwater. A satellite radar altimeter does the same with radio pulses: it bounces them off the sea and times how long they take to come back. Since TOPEX/Poseidon launched in 1992, a line of these satellites has flown the same track, repeating it every ten days. They measure sea level to within a few centimeters for 90% of the ocean.

cards.headline: Heat and color from above
cards.body: Other satellite sensors read the temperature of the sea surface, which reveals cold upwelling water and warm currents such as the Gulf Stream. Ocean-color sensors spot blooms of algae, the plankton whose chlorophyll can tint the sea green (Level 7), and help forecast where a bloom will drift.

cards.headline: Robots below the surface
cards.body: Satellites only see the sea's skin, so the Argo program sends down thousands of robot floats. Each drifts about 1 km deep. Every ten days it sinks to 2 km, then rises, measuring temperature and salinity, and radios its data to a satellite. It changes depth by pumping oil in and out of an outside bladder: Level 87's ballast trick. Argo is named for Jason's ship, because the floats work with the Jason satellites.

mascot.line: Satellites above, floats below, and a Greek myth holding them together. Oceanographers love a good pun.

cards.headline: Satellites: in orbit
learned: The Pacific sits about 20 cm above the Atlantic
Altimeters time radio echoes: sea level to a few cm
Satellites also read temperature and color
Argo floats measure down to 2 km

questions.prompt: How does a satellite radar altimeter measure the height of the sea?

options.label: It photographs the waves from above
It times radio pulses bounced off the sea surface
It drops floats that report their depth
options.rationale: That's Argo, working below the surface.

questions.explanation: The altimeter bounces radio pulses off the sea and times their return, which gives the sea's height.

questions.prompt: Satellites already watch the whole ocean. Why does the Argo program still need floats?

options.label: Satellites can't see ocean color
options.rationale: They can; ocean-color sensors do exactly that.

options.label: Satellites only see the surface; floats measure down to 2 km
Floats measure sea level more precisely from orbit
options.rationale: Floats work in the water, not in orbit.

options.label: Floats are needed to launch the satellites
options.rationale: They're separate tools that work together.

questions.explanation: Satellites see only the sea's surface; Argo floats measure temperature and salinity from 2 km up to the top.

questions.prompt: An Argo float sinks and rises by pumping oil in and out of an outside bladder. Which Level 87 idea is it using?

options.label: Nuclear power, like Nautilus under the Pole
options.rationale: Floats run on batteries and a pump.

options.label: A gasoline-filled float, like Trieste's
options.rationale: It pumps oil to change buoyancy, not a gasoline float.

options.label: A propeller pointed straight down at the floor
options.rationale: Floats have no propeller; they change buoyancy.

questions.explanation: Like ballast tanks, the bladder changes the float's buoyancy so it sinks or rises.
